paper.abstract:
Abstract Custom diffusion models (CDMs) have garnered significant interest owing to their remarkable capacity for generating personalized concepts. However, the majority of CDMs unrealistically presume that the user’s collection of personalized concepts is static and incapable of incremental growth over time. Furthermore, they exhibit significant catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect of previously learned concepts when incrementally learning a sequence of new ones. To resolve the above challenges, we develop a novel C ontinually C ustomizable D iffusion M odel (CCDM), enabling users to perform concept-incremental versatile customization. Specifically, we design an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module and a relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy
to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. They can preserve concept-specific attributes of each task and leverage beneficial inter-task correlations to enhance the continual learning of new customization tasks. Additionally, to address the challenge of concept neglect, we propose a controllable regional context synthesis strategy that performs multi-concept composition in alignment with user-provided conditions. This strategy enhances the overall consistency in multi-concept synthesis by guaranteeing semantic independence between user-defined regions and their smooth boundary transitions.
Experiments show our CCDM exhibits significant improvements over baseline methods.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Latent diffusion models (LDMs) [ 50 , 79 , 24 ] have emerged as an effective approach for high-quality content generation across various domains, including text-to-image synthesis [ 88 ] , video generation [ 76 ] , and 3D object creation [ 83 ] . By encoding input data into a latent space using a pretrained autoencoder, LDMs perform the denoising-based diffusion process in a lower-dimensional domain [ 47 ] . This design significantly reduces computational and memory costs while preserving the semantic richness required for photorealistic generation [ 28 , 21 ] . Despite their impressive performance, standard LDMs are typically trained on large-scale, general-purpose datasets [ 46 , 68 ] and struggle to synthesize user-specific concepts without extensive retraining. To address this limitation, custom diffusion models (CDMs) [ 82 , 25 , 44 , 20 ] have become a promising paradigm by using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 23 ] to finetune LDMs [ 46 , 3 ] on users’ personalized concepts. They expand the visual-language vocabulary of pretrained LDMs [ 88 ] by associating user-defined concepts with desired subjects [ 52 , 34 ] . Fig. 1: Illustration of the proposed CIVC problem. Fig. 2: Demonstration of our model’s scalability in supporting versatile concept customization tasks, including single/multi-concept synthesis, editing, and style transfer across text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D domains under the CIVC problem. Typically, the majority of CDMs [ 56 , 77 , 49 ] are built on the assumption that the set of each user’s personalized concepts remains constant and cannot continuously expand over time. However, this assumption contradicts practical scenarios, where users require a growing collection of new personalized concepts and wish to continually generate new concepts to reflect their evolving life experiences. To address such scenarios, existing CDMs [ 5 , 39 , 43 , 26 ] often rely on retaining all training data of previously learned concepts and leverage LoRA [ 23 ] to finetune pretrained LDMs [ 37 , 24 , 76 ] . Yet, as the volume of learned concepts accumulates, this strategy renders CDMs increasingly computationally intensive and more vulnerable to serious privacy issues [ 65 ] . If existing CDMs store all previously acquired low-rank parameters associated with old concepts and linearly fuse them for the continual learning of new concepts [ 78 , 90 ] , they may suffer from substantial degradation in their ability to preserve the distinctive characteristics of old personalized concepts, thereby hindering versatile concept customization [ 60 ] . This phenomenon is widely known as catastrophic forgetting of previously learned concepts [ 18 ] . Furthermore, in practical applications, users often seek precise control over the subjects and contexts linked to multiple previously learned concepts within generated images, videos, or 3D scenes for multi-concept composition, using conditions they provide (such as bounding boxes and scribbles [ 17 ] ). This requirement poses a significant challenge to CDMs [ 82 ] , which frequently face the issue of concept neglect [ 4 ] , whereby certain old concepts fail to appear during the synthesis of multiple concepts. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , CIVC enables CDMs [ 52 ] to continually learn and generate a series of new personalized concepts in a concept-incremental manner, while also supporting versatile concept customization tasks, including single/multi-concept synthesis, editing and style transfer across text-to-image [ 92 ] , text-to-video [ 26 ] and text-to-3D [ 44 ] domains. Our work significantly differs from existing baselines and offers strong scalability to perform a variety of different concept customization tasks (see Tab. I ). Additionally, during multi-concept composition, it allows users to guide the generation process by specifying the desired contexts, objects, and their intended spatial locations. Overall, the CIVC problem proposed in this paper faces the following two challenges: • Catastrophic Forgetting refers to the substantial loss of unique attributes of old concepts when existing CDMs [ 56 , 49 , 78 ] linearly merge their low-rank weights to incrementally learn new concepts. If new concepts ( e.g. , golden retriever) are semantically similar to previously learned ones ( e.g. , labrador retriever), CDMs tend to exhibit more severe forgetting of those old concepts. • Concept Neglect indicates the failure of some intended concepts to be properly synthesized at user-specified spatial locations during multi-concept composition. As multiple personalized concepts are composed together within generated images, videos, or 3D scenes, the risk increases that certain concepts may be overlooked, incorrectly blended, or visually overshadowed by others. To address the challenges of catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect in CIVC, we propose a novel C ontinually C ustomizable D iffusion M odel (CCDM) in this work. Firstly , we develop an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module and a relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy to alleviate catastrophic forgetting of previous concepts. The AD-LoRA module is designed to automatically retain concept-specific attributes while filtering out redundant characteristics. This is achieved by masking the LoRA parameters corresponding to irrelevant properties. By assessing semantic relevance, the relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy dynamically fuses low-rank updates from both current and previous tasks, exploiting beneficial inter-task correlations to facilitate the continual learning of new customization tasks. Secondly , to address concept neglect during multi-concept composition, we design a controllable regional context synthesis strategy that controls generated contexts to meet user-specified conditions. This module leverages a unified attention mask to restrict self-attention among image features exclusively to user-specified concept regions, while allowing cross-attention from image features to the textual embeddings of those regions. It promotes semantic independence across regions and seamless transitions at their boundaries, enhancing the holistic consistency of multi-concept synthesis. Comprehensive evaluations verify the efficacy of our CCDM in addressing diverse CIVC tasks across text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D domains (see Fig. 2 ). Our core contributions are listed as follows: • We formulate a practical Concept-Incremental Versatile Customization (CIVC) problem, characterized by challenges like catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect. • We design a novel Continually Customizable Diffusion Model (CCDM) to tackle the challenges of CIVC, enabling the continual customization of new concepts. • We propose attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) and relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation to alleviate catastrophic forgetting by retaining concept-specific attributes and exploiting positive inter-task correlations. • We develop a controllable regional context synthesis strategy to mitigate concept neglect in multi-concept generation by enabling semantic independence across regions and smooth transitions at their boundaries. Building upon our prior research [ 10 ] , this paper presents substantial improvements in both methodology and experiments: 1) Compared with [ 10 ] , we propose a novel attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module to identify which attributes of personalized concepts are distinctive. This AD-LoRA module preserves only the unique concept attributes to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. 2) The relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation merges the low-rank updates from current and previous tasks based on their semantic relevance. It explores positive inter-task relations to facilitate continual learning of new tasks. 3) We devise a controllable regional context synthesis strategy that uses a unified attention mask to limit self-attention to user-defined regions while enabling cross-attention to their textual embeddings for multi-concept synthesis. In contrast to [ 10 ] , it promotes greater semantic independence across regions and smoother transitions at their boundaries to tackle concept neglect. 4) We extend [ 10 ] to diverse CIVC tasks spanning text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D domains. 5) Our CCDM reduces the trainable parameters of [ 10 ] by 35% but achieves better customization performance than [ 10 ] . 6) More comparative evaluations, ablation results, and in-depth analyses are presented to prove the efficacy of our CCDM in handling the CIVC problem.

sections.heading: II Related Work
sections.text: Continual Learning (CL) [ 73 , 12 , 70 ] allows AI systems to continuously accumulate new knowledge from a stream of tasks while preserving previously learned information [ 1 ] . Modern regularization approaches impose optimization constraints on the weight updates of previous tasks to maintain previously learned knowledge [ 29 , 36 ] or apply knowledge distillation to facilitate knowledge propagation between new and old models [ 11 ] . Additionally, data replay methods maintain exemplars from previous categories [ 1 , 9 ] , or leverage generative architectures to synthesize data representing old classes [ 73 ] . These methods retrain AI systems from scratch using a combination of new-class data and synthesized data from old classes. Dynamic architectural approaches progressively adapt their structures to continually assimilate new classes [ 86 , 12 ] , while representation-based methods utilize prompt learning [ 70 ] or contrastive learning [ 45 ] to alleviate forgetting. Moreover, CL has been applied to a variety of vision tasks, including object recognition [ 86 ] , scene understanding [ 64 ] , and multi-modal reasoning [ 41 ] . Despite their effectiveness in visual domains, most CL methods [ 64 , 12 , 9 ] cannot be directly applied to solve the continual concept customization task ( e.g. , the CIVC problem). Concept Customization [ 91 , 5 , 3 , 43 , 71 ] refers to the process of extending pretrained LDMs [ 55 , 24 ] to generate user-defined personalized concepts. Following [ 56 ] , which addresses subject-driven synthesis by finetuning the full set of parameters in LDMs [ 3 ] , Gal et al. leverage textual inversion [ 14 ] to encode personalized concepts into learnable word embeddings for text-to-image concept customization. [ 30 ] enables the simultaneous training of multiple concepts or the merging of distinct diffusion models through the optimization of cross-attention parameters for multi-concept composition. Inspired by [ 30 ] , [ 19 ] optimizes only the singular value decomposition of latent encoding parameters to enhance customization efficiency. Building upon prior works [ 42 , 14 ] , some researchers [ 71 , 77 , 85 , 34 , 66 ] have extended these methodologies to temporal domains for personalized text-to-video synthesis. DreamVideo [ 71 ] proposes a dual-phase training strategy that separates concept acquisition from motion modeling, and [ 5 ] is designed for multi-concept video customization. For text-to-3D generation [ 80 , 39 ] , several works [ 53 , 51 , 52 , 83 ] use 2D LDMs [ 58 , 16 ] as the backbone and apply pose control to 3D objects, while others [ 49 , 44 , 81 ] aim to incorporate implicit 3D priors to facilitate the generation process. Besides, [ 60 , 62 , 18 ] focus on continual customization tasks that continuously synthesize new concepts, yet they lack the ability to control generated contexts and are prone to concept neglect during multi-concept synthesis. To tackle this issue, [ 88 , 47 ] use regional conditions, such as bounding boxes, to guide composition. However, the above CDMs [ 20 , 30 , 80 ] fail to incrementally synthesize new concepts in CIVC scenarios, suffering from catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect.

sections.heading: III Preliminary and Problem Definition
sections.text: Preliminary: To steer the generation of images, latent diffusion models (LDMs) [ 58 , 79 , 16 , 55 ] utilize conditional cues such as textual descriptions or images. The diffusion process takes places in a latent space, where an encoder ℰ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{E}(\cdot) transforms inputs into latent representations, and a decoder 𝒟 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{D}(\cdot) reconstructs them into images. By finetuning pretrained LDMs [ 59 , 50 ] with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 23 , 40 ] , custom diffusion models (CDMs) [ 42 , 43 , 91 ] can learn user-specific concepts. For a personalized image 𝐱 \mathbf{x} paired with its corresponding text prompt 𝐩 \mathbf{p} , the encoder ℰ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{E}(\cdot) projects 𝐱 \mathbf{x} into a latent feature 𝐳 \mathbf{z} . The noisy version of 𝐳 \mathbf{z} at the t t -th ( t = 1 , … , T t=1,\dots,T ) timestep is denoted as 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} . The text prompt 𝐩 \mathbf{p} is then encoded into the textual embedding 𝐜 = Ψ ⁡ ( 𝐩 ) \mathbf{c}=\Psi(\mathbf{p}) using a pretrained text encoder Ψ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Psi(\cdot) (such as CLIP [ 54 ] ). As a result, at the t t -th timestep, the learning objective for the customized concept pair { 𝐱 , 𝐩 } \{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p}\} is defined as follows: ℒ CDMs = 𝔼 𝐳 ∼ ℰ ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) , 𝐜 , ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) , t ​ [ ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ′ ​ ( 𝐳 t | 𝐜 , t ) ‖ 2 2 ] , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDMs}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{c},\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}),t}[\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{c},t)\|_{2}^{2}], (1) where the denoising UNet ϵ θ ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}}(\cdot) progressively denoises 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} by estimating ϵ θ ′ ​ ( 𝐳 t | 𝐜 , t ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}}(\mathbf{z}_{t}|\mathbf{c},t) [ 56 , 87 ] , which is assumed to follow a Gaussian distribution ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) . Additionally, the parameters θ ′ = θ 0 + Δ ​ θ \theta^{\prime}=\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta are composed of two components: the pretrained weights θ 0 = { 𝐖 0 l } l = 1 L \theta_{0}=\{\mathbf{W}_{0}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} from LDMs [ 13 , 67 ] and the low-rank updates Δ ​ θ = { Δ ​ 𝐖 l } l = 1 L \Delta\theta=\{\Delta\mathbf{W}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} introduced by LoRA [ 23 ] . In the l l -th ( l = 1 , ⋯ , L l=1,\cdots,L ) transformer layer of ϵ θ ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}}(\cdot) , 𝐖 0 l , Δ ​ 𝐖 l ∈ ℝ a × b \mathbf{W}_{0}^{l},\Delta\mathbf{W}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times b} represent the pretrained parameters and low-rank weights. a a and b b indicate the number of rows and columns. Δ ​ 𝐖 l = 𝐀 l ​ 𝐁 l \Delta\mathbf{W}^{l}=\mathbf{A}^{l}\mathbf{B}^{l} can be factorized as the product of two low-rank matrices [ 56 ] : 𝐀 l ∈ ℝ a × r \mathbf{A}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times r} and 𝐁 l ∈ ℝ r × b \mathbf{B}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times b} , with the rank r r satisfying the constraint r ≪ min ⁡ ( a , b ) r\ll\min(a,b) . Nevertheless, existing CDMs [ 81 , 14 ] typically presume a fixed set of user-specific concepts, which does not align with practical scenarios where users often desire to consecutively incorporate new personalized concepts reflecting their evolving preferences [ 60 ] . Additionally, these models are notably vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting of previously learned concepts and the neglect of certain concepts [ 62 , 42 ] when adapting to an incrementally expanding set of personalized concepts for versatile customization [ 10 ] . Problem Definition: To tackle the aforementioned issues, this paper introduces an innovative problem termed Concept-Incremental Versatile Customization (CIVC). This problem involves a sequence of successive concept customization tasks, denoted as 𝒯 = { 𝒯 u } u = 1 U \mathcal{T}=\{\mathcal{T}_{u}\}_{u=1}^{U} , with U U indicating the total number of tasks. The u u -th task 𝒯 u = { 𝐱 u s , 𝐩 u s , 𝐲 u s } s = 1 N u \mathcal{T}_{u}=\{\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{y}_{u}^{s}\}_{s=1}^{N_{u}} comprises N u N_{u} triplet samples, each containing an image 𝐱 u s \mathbf{x}_{u}^{s} , a corresponding text prompt 𝐩 u s \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s} , and a concept token 𝐲 u s ∈ 𝒴 u \mathbf{y}_{u}^{s}\in\mathcal{Y}_{u} . Specifically, the text prompt 𝐩 u s \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s} describes the visual content of 𝐱 u s \mathbf{x}_{u}^{s} ( e.g. , “photo of a [ V ∗ V_{*} ] [ V cat V_{\mathrm{cat}} ] drinking a cup of beer”), while 𝐲 u s \mathbf{y}_{u}^{s} is the conceptual element (such as [ V ∗ V_{*} ] [ V cat V_{\mathrm{cat}} ]) extracted from 𝐩 u s \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s} . The concept space 𝒴 u \mathcal{Y}_{u} for the u u -th learning task contains C u C_{u} new concepts, defined as 𝐲 u = ∪ s = 1 N u 𝐲 u s \mathbf{y}_{u}=\cup_{s=1}^{N_{u}}\mathbf{y}_{u}^{s} . In the CIVC setting, the concept spaces of distinct tasks are completely disjoint: 𝒴 u ∩ ( ∪ i = 1 u − 1 𝒴 i ) = ∅ \mathcal{Y}_{u}\cap(\cup_{i=1}^{u{-}1}\mathcal{Y}_{i})=\emptyset . This indicates that the C u C_{u} new personalized concepts introduced in the u u -th task are entirely distinct from the K u − 1 = ∑ i = 1 u − 1 C i K_{u{-}1}=\sum_{i=1}^{u{-}1}C_{i} previous concepts accumulated from the preceding u − 1 u{-}1 tasks. As shown in Tab. 1 , based on individual user preferences, each task 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} belongs to one of the diverse customization tasks: single/multi-concept synthesis, editing and style transfer across text-to-image [ 19 ] , text-to-video [ 75 ] and text-to-3D [ 61 ] domains. This is also referred to as versatile customization, which is the main focus of this paper. To satisfy the practical requirements of CIVC, no memory is reserved for archiving or reconstructing the training sets { 𝒯 u } u = 1 U \{\mathcal{T}_{u}\}_{u=1}^{U} across all tasks. This design ensures that all customization tasks adhere strictly to the concept-incremental learning paradigm. The CIVC setting aims to facilitate continual learning of new personalized concepts to meet diverse customization needs, while effectively tackling catastrophic forgetting of previous concepts and the challenge of concept neglect.

sections.heading: IV The Proposed Model
sections.text: In this section, as shown in Figs. 3 - 4 , we first use text-to-image customization as a representative example to illustrate the pipeline of our CCDM, which resolves the challenges of catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect in the CIVC problem. Specifically, we propose an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module (Sec. IV-A ) and a relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy (Sec. IV-B ) to overcome catastrophic forgetting, while also designing a controllable regional context synthesis strategy (Sec. IV-C ) to alleviate concept neglect during multi-concept generation. Then, we discuss how to extend our CCDM to text-to-video (Sec. IV-D ) and text-to-3D (Sec. IV-E ) customization under the CIVC setting. Fig. 3: Demonstration of (a) the attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module and (b) the relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy, using text-to-image customization as an example to illustrate the pipeline of our CCDM for mitigating catastrophic forgetting in the CIVC setting.

sections.heading: IV-A Attribute-Decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA)
sections.text: To enable the pretrained denoising UNet ϵ θ 0 ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot) to learn the u u -th concept customization task 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} , CDMs [ 57 , 48 , 74 , 50 , 92 ] employ LoRA [ 23 ] to finetune the model on personalized data 𝒯 u = { 𝐱 u s , 𝐩 u s , 𝐲 u s } s = 1 N u \mathcal{T}_{u}=\{\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{y}_{u}^{s}\}_{s=1}^{N_{u}} . This process involves optimizing the objective in Eq. ( 1 ), resulting in an updated denoising UNet ϵ θ u ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}_{u}}(\cdot) . Here, θ u ′ = θ 0 + Δ ​ θ u \theta^{\prime}_{u}=\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{u} , Δ ​ θ u = { Δ ​ 𝐖 u l } l = 1 L \Delta\theta_{u}=\{\Delta\mathbf{W}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} , and Δ ​ 𝐖 u l = 𝐀 u l ​ 𝐁 u l ∈ ℝ a × b \Delta\mathbf{W}_{u}^{l}=\mathbf{A}_{u}^{l}\mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times b} represents the low-rank updates in the l l -th layer, with 𝐀 u l ∈ ℝ a × r \mathbf{A}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times r} and 𝐁 u l ∈ ℝ r × b \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times b} being the corresponding low-rank decomposition matrices. Previous studies [ 55 , 82 ] have demonstrated that Δ ​ θ u \Delta\theta_{u} effectively captures the majority of the personalized concept characteristics in 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} . To continually learn new customization tasks under the CIVC setting, existing CDMs [ 27 , 69 , 53 ] require retaining the low-rank weights { Δ ​ θ i } i = 1 u − 1 \{\Delta\theta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{u-1} from all preceding tasks and linearly combining them during training by assessing their respective contributions to the current task. Unfortunately, this linear combination of low-rank weights causes a significant degradation in their ability to capture the distinctive attributes of previous concepts, a phenomenon also known as catastrophic forgetting of old concepts [ 18 ] . In light of this, Dong et al. [ 10 ] aim to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during model training by simultaneously preserving task-specific and shared knowledge through a concept consolidation loss. However, this method fails to identify which attributes of personalized concepts are distinctive and which are irrelevant in each incremental task. Moreover, the orthogonal constraint in [ 10 ] is highly dependent on hyperparameter selection, which cannot guarantee the absence of negative interference from irrelevant attributes across different tasks. Under these circumstances, mistakenly extracting irrelevant attributes of personalized concepts from previous tasks can severely interfere with the discovery of inherent attributes in the current customization task, thereby exacerbating forgetting under the CIVC setting. To address the above issues, as shown in Fig. 3 , we propose layer-wise concept tokens to explore a wide range of diverse attributes for personalized concepts. Additionally, we develop an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module that selectively preserves task-specific distinctive attributes while discarding irrelevant properties by zeroing out their encoding parameters in the low-rank weights. During the process of capturing concept-unique attributes, we strive to maximize the orthogonality of AD-LoRA across different tasks, thereby minimizing the negative interference of irrelevant attributes from previous concepts on learning the current task. • Layer-Wise Concept Tokens: Unlike traditional textual inversion approaches [ 14 , 89 , 7 ] that apply an identical text prompt across all transformer layers of the pretrained UNet ϵ θ 0 ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot) , we propose layer-wise concept tokens to capture diverse properties of personalized concepts during each concept customization task. Specifically, within the u u -th task 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} , each input tuple { 𝐱 u s , 𝐩 u s , 𝐲 u s } \{\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{y}_{u}^{s}\} contains L L layer-wise text prompts { 𝐩 u s , l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s,l}\}_{l=1}^{L} . At the l l -th layer of ϵ θ u ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta_{u}^{\prime}}(\cdot) , the prompt 𝐩 u s , l \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s,l} is paired with a corresponding layer-wise concept token 𝐲 u s , l \mathbf{y}_{u}^{s,l} . To provide a concrete instance, when processing an image 𝐱 u s \mathbf{x}_{u}^{s} with its associated text prompt 𝐩 u s \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s} (“photo of a [ V ∗ V_{*} ] [ V cat V_{\mathrm{cat}} ] drinking a cup of beer”), the text prompt for the l l -th layer is expressed as 𝐩 u s , l \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s,l} (“photo of a [ V ∗ l V_{*}^{l} ] [ V cat l V_{\mathrm{cat}}^{l} ] drinking a cup of beer”), with the corresponding layer-wise concept token 𝐲 u s , l \mathbf{y}_{u}^{s,l} being [ V ∗ l V_{*}^{l} ] [ V cat l V_{\mathrm{cat}}^{l} ]. After 𝐩 u s \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s} is employed to initialize { 𝐩 u s , l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s,l}\}_{l=1}^{L} , the textual embedding 𝐜 u s , l = Ψ ⁡ ( 𝐩 u s , l ) ∈ ℝ N p × d \mathbf{c}_{u}^{s,l}=\Psi(\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s,l})\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times d} , obtained by encoding 𝐩 u s , l \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s,l} with the text encoder Ψ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Psi(\cdot) , is injected into the l l -th transformer layer of ϵ θ u ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta_{u}^{\prime}}(\cdot) via cross-attention. Here, N p N_{p} is the token length and d d refers to the feature dimension of the textual embedding. When incorporating LoRA and layer-wise concept tokens to optimize ϵ θ u ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}_{u}}(\cdot) via Eq. ( 1 ), we can obtain varied attributes of personalized concepts within the u u -th concept customization task. Nevertheless, it is challenging to manually determine which attributes of personalized concepts are distinctive and which are redundant in each customization task. Such irrelevant concept properties may hinder the continual learning of new tasks under the CIVC setting, thereby aggravating catastrophic forgetting of previously learned concepts. • AD-LoRA Module: To preserve concept-unique attributes while discarding irrelevant ones, we propose an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module. For the low-rank update Δ ​ 𝐖 u l = 𝐀 u l ​ 𝐁 u l \Delta\mathbf{W}_{u}^{l}=\mathbf{A}_{u}^{l}\mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} of the l l -th layer, we initialize 𝐀 u l \mathbf{A}_{u}^{l} by sampling from a standard Gaussian distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathcal{N}(0,1) and set 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} to zero, ensuring that Δ ​ 𝐖 u l = 0 \Delta\mathbf{W}_{u}^{l}=0 at the beginning of learning the u u -th task. Subsequently, we keep 𝐀 u l \mathbf{A}_{u}^{l} frozen and update only the key parameters of 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} that are responsible for capturing the distinctive properties of personalized concepts, while zeroing out the encoding parameters of irrelevant attributes to facilitate the learning of the u u -th task. To achieve this, we employ parameter importance calibration to derive a sparse mask 𝐌 u l ∈ ℝ r × b \mathbf{M}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times b} for 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} . This mask ensures that training updates are applied only to the parameters in 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} that are essential for learning the u u -th task. For parameter importance calibration, we first finetune { 𝐁 u l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} on the u u -th task 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} , and then use the first-order gradient updates of 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} at the m m -th iteration ( m = 200 m=200 ) to compute its Fisher information matrix 𝐅 u l ∈ ℝ r × b \mathbf{F}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times b} . It is worth noting that 𝐅 u l \mathbf{F}_{u}^{l} can evaluate the importance of each parameter in learning the u u -th task, where higher values correspond to greater importance. Subsequently, we arrange the absolute values of all elements from { 𝐅 u l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{F}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} in descending order to obtain 𝐅 u ∗ ∈ ℝ N b \mathbf{F}_{u}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{b}} , and use the sparsity ratio ρ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \rho\in(0,1) to select the element ranked at the ρ ​ N b \rho N_{b} -th position in 𝐅 u ∗ \mathbf{F}_{u}^{*} as the global threshold τ u \tau_{u} . Here, N b = r ​ b ​ L N_{b}=rbL is relatively small since r ≪ b r\ll b . As a result, at the u u -th task, the sparse mask 𝐌 u l ∈ ℝ r × b \mathbf{M}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times b} for the l l -th layer is defined as: 𝐌 u l = 𝕀 | 𝐅 u l | ≥ τ u , τ u = 𝐅 u ∗ ​ [ ρ ​ N b ] , \displaystyle\mathbf{M}_{u}^{l}=\mathbb{I}_{|\mathbf{F}_{u}^{l}|\geq\tau_{u}},~~\tau_{u}=\mathbf{F}_{u}^{*}[\rho N_{b}], (2) where 𝕀 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function that sets the corresponding values in 𝐌 u l \mathbf{M}_{u}^{l} to 1 if the absolute values of elements in 𝐅 u l \mathbf{F}_{u}^{l} exceed τ u \tau_{u} . Then, we apply 𝐌 u l \mathbf{M}_{u}^{l} to 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} to derive a new low-rank update Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l \Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l} for the l l -th layer at the u u -th task: Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l = 𝐀 u l ​ ( 𝐁 u l ⊙ 𝐌 u l ) , \displaystyle\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l}=\mathbf{A}_{u}^{l}(\mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}\odot\mathbf{M}_{u}^{l}), (3) where ⊙ \odot is the Hadamard product. Evidently, if the absolute values in 𝐅 u l \mathbf{F}_{u}^{l} exceed τ u \tau_{u} , the corresponding parameters in 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} are considered essential for capturing distinctive properties of the personalized concepts in the u u -th task and are retained by the mask 𝐌 u l \mathbf{M}_{u}^{l} . Otherwise, they are regarded as encoding irrelevant attributes and are masked out ( i.e. , set to zero). Orthogonality of AD-LoRA: The matrices { 𝐀 u l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{A}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} in Eq. ( 3 ), initialized from a Gaussian distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathcal{N}(0,1) and kept fixed during training, ensure that the low-rank updates across different layers are orthogonal for the u u -th customization task: ⟨ Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l , Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u γ ⟩ ≈ 0 \langle\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l},\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{\gamma}\rangle\approx 0 , where γ = 1 , ⋯ , L \gamma=1,\cdots,L and γ ≠ l \gamma\neq l . They also ensure that the low-rank updates for the u u -th task are approximately orthogonal to those of the i i -th ( i = 1 , ⋯ , u − 1 i=1,\cdots,u{-}1 ) previous task: ⟨ Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l , Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ i l ′ ⟩ ≈ 0 \langle\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l},\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}\rangle\approx 0 , where l ′ = 1 , ⋯ , L l^{\prime}=1,\cdots,L . The above strict orthogonality allows { Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l } l = 1 L \{\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} to capture distinctive properties of the u u -th task, while minimizing interference from irrelevant attributes both across layers in the current task and from previous tasks. However, such a strict orthogonality constraint may hinder the learning of semantically similar concepts with closely related attributes. Considering that adjacent layers tend to capture similar attributes, we fix the parameters of { 𝐀 u l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{A}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} in either the odd or even layers to address the above issue. It ensures orthogonality of AD-LoRA across non-adjacent layers and different tasks, which minimizes interference from irrelevant attributes of old concepts in learning new tasks. Proof: To prove ⟨ Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l , Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ i l ′ ⟩ ≈ 0 \langle\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l},\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}\rangle\approx 0 , we define Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ i l ′ = 𝐀 i l ′ ​ ( 𝐁 i l ′ ⊙ 𝐌 i l ′ ) \Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}=\mathbf{A}_{i}^{{l^{\prime}}}(\mathbf{B}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}\odot\mathbf{M}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}) via Eq. ( 3 ), and have the following deduction: ⟨ Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l , Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ i l ′ ⟩ \displaystyle\langle\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l},\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}\rangle = Tr ⁡ ( ( Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l ) ⊤ ​ Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ i l ′ ) \displaystyle=\mathrm{Tr}\big((\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l})^{\top}\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}\big) (4) = Tr ⁡ ( ( 𝐁 u l ⊙ 𝐌 u l ) ⊤ ​ ( 𝐀 u l ) ⊤ ​ 𝐀 i l ′ ​ ( 𝐁 i l ′ ⊙ 𝐌 i l ′ ) ) . \displaystyle=\mathrm{Tr}\big((\mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}\odot\mathbf{M}_{u}^{l})^{\top}(\mathbf{A}_{u}^{l})^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}(\mathbf{B}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}\odot\mathbf{M}_{i}^{l^{\prime}})\big). Following [ 15 ] , we demonstrate that when both 𝐀 i l ′ \mathbf{A}_{i}^{l^{\prime}} and 𝐀 u l \mathbf{A}_{u}^{l} are independently sampled from a high-dimensional standard Gaussian distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathcal{N}(0,1) , their inner product satisfies ⟨ 𝐀 u l , 𝐀 i l ′ ⟩ ≈ 0 \langle\mathbf{A}_{u}^{l},\mathbf{A}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}\rangle\approx 0 with high probability. This completes the proof that the orthogonality condition ⟨ Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l , Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ i l ′ ⟩ ≈ 0 \langle\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l},\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{i}^{l^{\prime}}\rangle\approx 0 in Eq. ( 4 ) holds. By analogous reasoning, we further verify the orthogonality relation ⟨ Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l , Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u γ ⟩ ≈ 0 \langle\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l},\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{\gamma}\rangle\approx 0 between the low-rank updates of different layers within the u u -th task.

sections.heading: IV-B Relevance-Guided AD-LoRA Aggregation
sections.text: Despite effectively capturing unique concept attributes within each task, the AD-LoRA module in Sec. IV-A cannot explore the underlying relationships between previously learned concepts and new concepts, nor can it use their positive relations to facilitate continual learning of new tasks in CIVC. To address the above issues, as shown in Fig. 3 , we propose relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation. It adaptively merges the low-rank updates from the new and previous tasks based on their semantic relevance, thereby fully leveraging positive inter-task relations to enhance the learning of the u u -th new task. Specifically, we preserve all task learners { 𝒵 i } i = 1 u − 1 \{\mathcal{Z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{u{-}1} learned from the previous ( u − 1 ) (u{-}1) tasks to learn the u u -th task, where 𝒵 i = { Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ i l , 𝐲 ^ i l } l = 1 L \mathcal{Z}_{i}=\{\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{i}^{l},\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} indicates the task learner of the i i -th task ( i = 1 , ⋯ , u − 1 i=1,\cdots,u{-}1 ), 𝐲 ^ i l = { 𝐲 ^ i l , k } k = 1 C i \widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{l}=\{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{l,k}\}_{k=1}^{C_{i}} , and 𝐲 ^ i l , k \widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{l,k} is the k k -th concept token acquired in the l l -th layer. As aforementioned in Sec. IV-A , at the u u -th customization task, given an input tuple { 𝐱 u s , 𝐩 u s , 𝐲 u s } ∈ 𝒯 u \{\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{y}_{u}^{s}\}\in\mathcal{T}_{u} during training, we utilize the text encoder Ψ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Psi(\cdot) to extract the layer-wise textual embedding 𝐜 u s , l = Ψ ⁡ ( 𝐩 u s , l ) ∈ ℝ N p × d \mathbf{c}_{u}^{s,l}=\Psi(\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s,l})\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times d} for the text prompt 𝐩 u s , l \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s,l} at the l l -th layer. Considering the set of stored task learners { 𝒵 i } i = 1 u − 1 \{\mathcal{Z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{u{-}1} , all concept tokens accumulated up to the current task can be represented as { Ω u − 1 l } l = 1 L \{\Omega_{u{-}1}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} , where Ω u − 1 l = ∪ i = 1 u − 1 𝐲 ^ i l ∈ ℝ K u − 1 \Omega_{u{-}1}^{l}=\cup_{i=1}^{u-1}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{u{-}1}} comprises K u − 1 = ∑ i = 1 u − 1 C i K_{u{-}1}=\sum_{i=1}^{u-1}C_{i} concept tokens derived from the l l -th layer of ϵ θ u ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta_{u}^{\prime}}(\cdot) . Subsequently, Ψ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Psi(\cdot) maps the set of concept tokens { Ω u − 1 l } l = 1 L \{\Omega_{u{-}1}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} to the corresponding latent representations { 𝐞 u − 1 l ∈ ℝ K u − 1 × d } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{e}_{u{-}1}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{u{-}1}\times d}\}_{l=1}^{L} . For each 𝐞 u − 1 l \mathbf{e}_{u{-}1}^{l} , the latent representations corresponding to the same task are averaged to derive a new representation 𝐞 ^ u − 1 l ∈ ℝ ( u − 1 ) × d \widehat{\mathbf{e}}_{u{-}1}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{(u{-}1)\times d} , where ( u − 1 ) (u{-}1) denotes the total number of previously learned tasks. Then we calculate the semantic affinity ℛ u − 1 l ∈ ℝ u − 1 \mathcal{R}_{u{-}1}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{u{-}1} between 𝐞 ^ u − 1 l \widehat{\mathbf{e}}_{u{-}1}^{l} and 𝐜 u s , l \mathbf{c}_{u}^{s,l} , and use ℛ u − 1 l \mathcal{R}_{u{-}1}^{l} to determine the indices β u − 1 l ∈ ℝ λ \beta_{u{-}1}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{\lambda} of the λ \lambda previous tasks ( λ ≤ u − 1 \lambda\leq u{-}1 ) that are most semantically similar to the u u -th task: β u − 1 l = max - idx [ 1 : λ ] ( ℛ u − 1 l ) , ℛ u − 1 l = max ( 𝐞 ^ u − 1 l ⋅ ( 𝐜 u s , l ) ⊤ ) , \displaystyle\!\!\beta_{u{-}1}^{l}\!=\!\mathrm{max}\text{-}\mathrm{idx}_{[1:\lambda]}(\mathcal{R}_{u{-}1}^{l}),\mathcal{R}_{u{-}1}^{l}\!=\!\max\!\big(\widehat{\mathbf{e}}_{u{-}1}^{l}\!\cdot\!(\mathbf{c}_{u}^{s,l})^{\top}\big),\!\! (5) where max ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \max(\cdot) selects the maximum value in each row, and max - idx [ 1 : λ ] ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{max}\text{-}\mathrm{idx}_{[1:\lambda]}(\cdot) obtains the indices of top λ \lambda maximum values. Subsequently, we leverage the underlying semantic relationships between the new task and the λ \lambda selected previous tasks to facilitate the learning of the u u -th task during training. Specifically, at the l l -th layer, we dynamically merge their low-rank updates to obtain a new update Δ ​ 𝐖 ~ u l \Delta\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l} by adaptively learning the combination weights within the network itself: Δ ​ 𝐖 ~ u l \displaystyle\Delta\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l} = ∑ i = 1 λ + 1 σ ​ ( 𝐖 p l ​ 𝐄 ​ ( 𝐱 u s ) ) i ⋅ Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ ξ i l \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda+1}\sigma(\mathbf{W}_{p}^{l}\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s}))_{i}\cdot\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{\xi_{i}}^{l} = ∑ i = 1 λ + 1 σ ​ ( 𝐖 p l ​ 𝐄 ​ ( 𝐱 u s ) ) i ⋅ 𝐀 ξ i l ​ ( 𝐁 ξ i l ⊙ 𝐌 ξ i l ) , \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda+1}\sigma(\mathbf{W}_{p}^{l}\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s}))_{i}\cdot\mathbf{A}_{\xi_{i}}^{l}(\mathbf{B}_{\xi_{i}}^{l}\odot\mathbf{M}_{\xi_{i}}^{l}), (6) where ξ i = β u − 1 l ​ [ i ] \xi_{i}=\beta_{u{-}1}^{l}[i] denotes the i i -th element of β u − 1 l \beta_{u{-}1}^{l} . To learn the low-rank updates Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l {\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l}} for the u u -th task, we include the current task index by setting β u − 1 l ​ [ λ + 1 ] = u \beta_{u{-}1}^{l}[\lambda{+}1]=u , resulting in β u − 1 l ∈ ℝ λ + 1 \beta_{u{-}1}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{\lambda{+}1} . 𝐄 ⁡ ( 𝐱 u s ) ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the global feature of given image 𝐱 u s \mathbf{x}_{u}^{s} , 𝐖 p l ∈ ℝ ( λ + 1 ) × d \mathbf{W}_{p}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{(\lambda+1)\times d} is a trainable projection matrix, and σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) denotes the softmax function. σ ​ ( 𝐖 p l ​ 𝐄 ​ ( 𝐱 u s ) ) i \sigma(\mathbf{W}_{p}^{l}\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s}))_{i} represents the i i -th element of σ ⁡ ( 𝐖 p l ​ 𝐄 ​ ( 𝐱 u s ) ) ∈ ℝ λ + 1 \sigma(\mathbf{W}_{p}^{l}\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s}))\in\mathbb{R}^{\lambda+1} . As a result, for the denoising UNet ϵ θ u ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}_{u}}(\cdot) at the u u -th task, the parameter update Δ ​ θ u \Delta\theta_{u} can be reformulated as Δ ​ θ u = { Δ ​ 𝐖 ~ u l } l = 1 L \Delta\theta_{u}=\{\Delta\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} . Optimization: When learning the u u -th concept customization task, we freeze the parameters ⋃ i = 1 λ { Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ ξ i l } l = 1 L \bigcup_{i=1}^{\lambda}\{\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{\xi_{i}}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} from the λ \lambda selected previous tasks, and optimize only the low-rank weights { Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l } l = 1 L \{\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} and the learnable projection matrices { 𝐖 p l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{W}_{p}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} of the u u -th task during training. This freezing operation prevents the overwriting of previously acquired knowledge, while exploiting the positive relationships between new and old tasks to learn task-specific knowledge for the u u -th task, thereby mitigating the catastrophic forgetting of previously learned personalized concepts. In addition, selecting only the λ \lambda most semantically similar tasks, instead of all tasks, improves training efficiency. After determining the mask 𝐌 u l \mathbf{M}_{u}^{l} via Eq. ( 2 ), the optimization update of 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} at the l l -th layer of the UNet ϵ θ u ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}_{u}}(\cdot) is formulated as follows: 𝐁 u l ← 𝐁 u l − ϑ ⋅ ( ( ∇ 𝐁 u l ℒ CDMs ) ⊙ 𝐌 u l ) , \displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}\leftarrow\mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}-\vartheta\cdot\big((\nabla_{\mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CDMs}})\odot\mathbf{M}_{u}^{l}\big), (7) where ϑ \vartheta denotes the learning rate to update 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} in this paper. Inference: Upon completing the learning of the u u -th task, we store its task learner 𝒵 u = { Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ u l , 𝐲 ^ u l } l = 1 L \mathcal{Z}_{u}=\{\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{u}^{l},\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} and merge it with the learners from previously learned tasks to form { 𝒵 i } i = 1 u \{\mathcal{Z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{u} for inference. It is worth noting that the memory overhead required to retain 𝒵 i \mathcal{Z}_{i} (where i i ranges from 1 1 to u u ) constitutes only 0.15% of the total memory of ϵ θ 0 ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot) , which does not affect the practical deployment of CIVC. Given the text prompt for inference, denoted as 𝐩 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{p}} , we employ it to initialize a set of layer-wise text prompts { 𝐩 ^ l } l = 1 L \{\widehat{\mathbf{p}}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} . These layer-wise prompts are then processed by the text encoder Ψ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Psi(\cdot) to extract their corresponding textual embeddings 𝐜 ^ = { 𝐜 ^ l ∈ ℝ N p × d } l = 1 L \widehat{\mathbf{c}}=\{\widehat{\mathbf{c}}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}\times d}\}_{l=1}^{L} . Subsequently, we collect K u = ∑ i = 1 u C i K_{u}=\sum_{i=1}^{u}C_{i} concept tokens from the u u task learners { 𝒵 i } i = 1 u \{\mathcal{Z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{u} to obtain { Ω u l } l = 1 L \{\Omega_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} , where Ω u l = ∪ i = 1 u 𝐲 ^ i l ∈ ℝ K u \Omega_{u}^{l}=\cup_{i=1}^{u}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{u}} . After projecting { Ω u l } l = 1 L \{\Omega_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} into latent textual embeddings via Ψ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Psi(\cdot) and averaging the embeddings corresponding to the same task to obtain { 𝐞 ^ u l ∈ ℝ u × d } l = 1 L \{\widehat{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{u\times d}\}_{l=1}^{L} , we measure the semantic correlations ℛ u l = max ⁡ ( 𝐞 ^ u l ⋅ ( 𝐜 ^ l ) ⊤ ) ∈ ℝ u \mathcal{R}_{u}^{l}=\max(\widehat{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{l}\cdot(\widehat{\mathbf{c}}^{l})^{\top})\in\mathbb{R}^{u} between 𝐞 ^ u l \widehat{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{l} and 𝐜 ^ l \widehat{\mathbf{c}}^{l} . Then, ℛ u l \mathcal{R}_{u}^{l} is utilized to select the indices β u l = max - idx [ 1 : λ ] ( ℛ u l ) ∈ ℝ λ \beta_{u}^{l}=\mathrm{max}\text{-}\mathrm{idx}_{[1:\lambda]}(\mathcal{R}_{u}^{l})\in\mathbb{R}^{\lambda} of the λ \lambda learned tasks that are most semantically similar to the given text prompt 𝐩 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{p}} . Since the given text prompt 𝐩 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{p}} is variable during testing and may differ from the training samples, we cannot store its corresponding projection matrices { 𝐖 p l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{W}_{p}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} to fuse the low-rank weights of the λ \lambda selected tasks via Eq. ( 6 ) for inference. To tackle this issue, we concatenate the semantic affinities of the λ \lambda selected tasks to obtain ℳ l = { ℛ u l ​ [ ξ i ] } i = 1 λ ∈ ℝ λ \mathcal{M}^{l}=\{\mathcal{R}_{u}^{l}[\xi_{i}]\}_{i=1}^{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{\lambda} , where ξ i = β u l ​ [ i ] \xi_{i}=\beta_{u}^{l}[i] and ℛ u l ​ [ ξ i ] \mathcal{R}_{u}^{l}[\xi_{i}] denotes the ξ i \xi_{i} -th element of ℛ u l \mathcal{R}_{u}^{l} . Subsequently, we employ ℳ l \mathcal{M}^{l} to adaptively combine the low-rank weights of λ \lambda selected tasks, yielding a new low-rank weight Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ ∗ l \Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{*}^{l} at the l l -th transformer layer for inference: Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ ∗ l = ∑ i = 1 λ ψ ​ ( ℳ l ) i ⋅ 𝐀 ξ i l ​ ( 𝐁 ξ i l ⊙ 𝐌 ξ i l ) , \displaystyle\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{*}^{l}=\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda}\psi(\mathcal{M}^{l})_{i}\cdot\mathbf{A}_{\xi_{i}}^{l}(\mathbf{B}_{\xi_{i}}^{l}\odot\mathbf{M}_{\xi_{i}}^{l}), (8) where ψ ⁡ ( ℳ l ) = ( ℳ l ) 2 / ‖ ( ℳ l ) 2 ‖ F ∈ ℝ λ \psi(\mathcal{M}^{l})=(\mathcal{M}^{l})^{2}/\|(\mathcal{M}^{l})^{2}\|_{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{\lambda} aims to normalize ℳ l \mathcal{M}^{l} , and ψ ​ ( ℳ l ) i \psi(\mathcal{M}^{l})_{i} denotes the i i -th entry of ψ ⁡ ( ℳ l ) \psi(\mathcal{M}^{l}) . After obtaining the new low-rank weights { Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ ∗ l } l = 1 L \{\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{*}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} across different layers via Eq. ( 8 ), we derive a new denoising UNet ϵ θ ∗ ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta_{*}^{\prime}}(\cdot) for inference. Here, θ ∗ ′ = θ 0 + Δ ​ θ ∗ \theta^{\prime}_{*}=\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{*} and Δ ​ θ ∗ = { Δ ​ 𝐖 ^ ∗ l } l = 1 L \Delta\theta_{*}=\{\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{W}}_{*}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} . It is worth mentioning that θ ∗ ′ \theta^{\prime}_{*} captures the task-specific distinctive properties of all learned personalized concepts that are semantically close to the given text prompt 𝐩 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{p}} , while discarding their irrelevant attributes under the CIVC setting. As a result, θ ∗ ′ \theta^{\prime}_{*} plays a critical role in addressing catastrophic forgetting of previously learned concepts during inference. sections.heading: IV-C Controllable Regional Context Synthesis
sections.text: Under the CIVC setting, directly applying ϵ θ ∗ ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}_{*}}(\cdot) obtained in Sec. IV-B for multi-concept customization fails to produce high-quality images that adhere to user-specified conditions (such as bounding boxes [ 33 , 35 ] ). This is because the generation of certain personalized concepts within specified regions is often overlooked, a phenomenon referred to as concept neglect [ 4 ] . To mitigate concept neglect, several studies [ 10 , 17 ] propose regional cross-attention between the image feature map and textual embeddings, aiming to independently associate each intended concept with its corresponding user-provided region. However, they fail to maintain seamless transitions at the boundaries of different bounding boxes within the holistic composition. To address this issue, we develop a controllable regional context synthesis module, as depicted in Fig. 4 . It uses a unified attention mask to restrict self-attention among image features to user-provided regions, while enabling cross-attention from image features to region textual embeddings. This module guarantees the semantic independence of distinct bounding boxes and facilitates smooth transitions at their boundaries, thereby enhancing the overall consistency of multi-concept composition. • Regional Concept Generation: In addition to the base text prompt (BTP) 𝐩 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{p}} introduced in Sec. IV-B , users can also specify η \eta region conditions, denoted as { 𝐩 ^ w , 𝐛 ^ w } w = 1 η \{\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{w},\widehat{\mathbf{b}}_{w}\}_{w=1}^{\eta} , to control the context of multi-concept customization. Here, 𝐩 ^ w \widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{w} is the w w -th regional text prompt (RTP), which is used to generate the corresponding concept within the bounding box 𝐛 ^ w ∈ ℝ 4 \widehat{\mathbf{b}}_{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{4} . The text encoder Ψ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Psi(\cdot) is employed to derive the layer-wise textual embeddings 𝐜 ^ w = { 𝐜 ^ w l ∈ ℝ N w × d } l = 1 L \widehat{\mathbf{c}}_{w}=\{\widehat{\mathbf{c}}_{w}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{w}\times d}\}_{l=1}^{L} for 𝐩 ^ w \widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{w} , where N w N_{w} is the prompt length of 𝐩 ^ w \widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{w} . Subsequently, the new denoising UNet ϵ θ ∗ ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}_{*}}(\cdot) acquired from Sec. IV-B extracts layer-wise image features { 𝐟 l ∈ ℝ h l × w l × d } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{f}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{h^{l}\times w^{l}\times d}\}_{l=1}^{L} by incorporating with the base text prompt 𝐩 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{p}} . h l h^{l} and w l w^{l} represent the height and width of 𝐟 l \mathbf{f}^{l} . To improve the holistic coherence of multi-concept composition, we concatenate 𝐟 l \mathbf{f}^{l} with all region textual embeddings { 𝐜 ^ w l } w = 1 η \{\widehat{\mathbf{c}}_{w}^{l}\}_{w=1}^{\eta} to obtain 𝐟 ^ r l ∈ ℝ N f l × d \widehat{\mathbf{f}}_{r}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{f}^{l}\times d} at the l l -th layer of ϵ θ ∗ ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}_{*}}(\cdot) , and define its unified attention mask as 𝐦 ^ r l ∈ ℝ N f l × N f l \widehat{\mathbf{m}}_{r}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{f}^{l}\times N_{f}^{l}} , where N f l = h l ​ w l + ∑ w = 1 η N w N_{f}^{l}=h^{l}w^{l}+\sum_{w=1}^{\eta}N_{w} . sections.heading: IV-D Extension to Text-to-Video Customization
sections.text: To extend the proposed CCDM to text-to-video customization under the CIVC setting, we introduce 5 motion concepts (V31–V35), in addition to the 30 subject concepts (V1–V30) used for text-to-image synthesis, as shown in Fig. 6 . Specifically, we apply the proposed CCDM to the CogVideoX backbone [ 84 ] to continually learn subject and motion concepts. Similar to text-to-image customization, when learning the u u -th task 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} , we initialize L L layer-wise text prompts { 𝐩 u s , l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s,l}\}_{l=1}^{L} and L L corresponding layer-wise concept tokens { 𝐲 u s , l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{y}_{u}^{s,l}\}_{l=1}^{L} for each input tuple { 𝐱 u s , 𝐩 u s , 𝐲 u s } \{\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{y}_{u}^{s}\} . Following Dualreal [ 66 ] , we apply AD-LoRA to the spatial transformer blocks of CogVideoX for learning subject concepts and to the temporal transformer blocks for learning motion concepts. Furthermore, we implement the proposed relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy in both spatial and temporal transformer blocks, with each component optimized independently to learn subject and motion concepts, respectively. For multi-concept text-to-video customization, users can also provide a specific motion trajectory for each regional text prompt to control the generated contexts of videos. As presented in Fig. 5 , given the w w -th regional text prompt 𝐩 ^ w \widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{w} and its motion trajectory, we automatically place a bounding box at each position along the motion trajectory to obtain frame-level bounding boxes 𝐛 ^ w ∈ ℝ n v × 4 \widehat{\mathbf{b}}_{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{v}\times 4} for 𝐩 ^ w \widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{w} . Here, n v n_{v} is the number of frames in the synthesized video. Given η \eta region conditions { 𝐩 ^ w , 𝐛 ^ w } w = 1 η \{\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{w},\widehat{\mathbf{b}}_{w}\}_{w=1}^{\eta} and a base text prompt 𝐩 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{p}} , we first use 𝐩 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{p}} to extract layer-wise video features { 𝐟 l ∈ ℝ n v × h l × w l × d } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{f}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{v}\times h^{l}\times w^{l}\times d}\}_{l=1}^{L} via the denoising UNet ϵ θ ∗ ′ ​ ( ⋅ ) \epsilon_{\theta^{\prime}_{*}}(\cdot) in Sec. IV-B . For the i i -th frame ( i = 1 , ⋯ , n v i=1,\cdots,n_{v} ), we utilize the frame feature 𝐟 l ​ [ i ] ∈ ℝ h l × w l × d \mathbf{f}^{l}[i]\in\mathbb{R}^{h^{l}\times w^{l}\times d} together with the corresponding region conditions { 𝐩 ^ w , 𝐛 ^ w ​ [ i ] } w = 1 η \{\widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{w},\widehat{\mathbf{b}}_{w}[i]\}_{w=1}^{\eta} to execute the proposed controllable regional context synthesis module (Sec. IV-C ) within the l l -th spatial transformer block, analogous to text-to-image customization. 𝐛 ^ w ​ [ i ] ∈ ℝ 4 \widehat{\mathbf{b}}_{w}[i]\in\mathbb{R}^{4} is the bounding box of the regional text prompt 𝐩 ^ w \widehat{\mathbf{p}}_{w} at the i i -th frame. sections.heading: V-A Implementation Details
sections.text: Dataset: Drawing motivation from previous methods [ 10 , 62 , 60 , 30 ] , we propose a novel concept-incremental learning (CIL) benchmark to evaluate model performance in text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D concept customization under the CIVC setting. Specifically, this benchmark comprises 20 object concepts, 5 style concepts (V6, V8, V10, V17 and V20), 5 person concepts (V15, V22, V23, V26 and V28), and 5 motion concepts (V31–V35), resulting in a total of 35 personalized concepts. Under the CIVC setting, as presented in Fig. 6 , we utilize 30 continual concept generation tasks (V1–V30), excluding motion concepts, for both text-to-image and text-to-3D customization, while all concepts (V1–V35) are used for text-to-video customization. To reflect real-world CIVC scenarios, each task contains approximately 3–5 text-image pairs, with text prompts generated using BLIP [ 32 ] . More importantly, we intentionally include several semantically similar concepts ( e.g. , V1, V7, V18, and V19 dogs; V4 and V11 backpacks; V3 and V9 cats) to increase the difficulty and challenge of the proposed CIL benchmark. Experimental Setups: Following [ 67 ] , we adopt SDXL [ 50 ] and FLUX.1 [ 31 ] as the backbone architectures for text-to-image customization, CogVideoX [ 84 ] for text-to-video customization, and SDXL [ 50 ] for text-to-3D customization. To ensure fairness, all state-of-the-art baselines and our proposed model are trained under identical settings, including the same backbone and the Adam optimizer. The learning rates are configured as 1.0 × 10 − 3 1.0\times 10^{-3} for textual embedding updates and 1.0 × 10 − 4 1.0\times 10^{-4} for the denoising optimization of UNet. Following [ 31 , 10 ] , we set the low-rank parameter to r = 8 r=8 for FLUX.1 and SDXL while configuring r = 32 r=32 for CogVideoX. Furthermore, we set ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 to mask 20% of the trainable parameters in 𝐁 u l \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l} , and μ = 0.1 \mu=0.1 in Eq. ( 14 ). Additionally, based on empirical results in Tab. VI , we fix the parameters of { 𝐀 u l } l = 1 L \{\mathbf{A}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} in the even layers. To showcase our model’s superiority in addressing the CIVC problem, we evaluate it against eight state-of-the-art methods spanning three categories: 1) continual learning approaches (LWF [ 36 ] and EWC [ 29 ] ); 2) multi-LoRA integration methods (LoRA-M [ 90 ] and LoRA-C [ 90 ] ); and 3) continual diffusion models (L2DM [ 62 ] , CLoRA [ 60 ] , CIDM [ 10 ] and CPG [ 18 ] ). For fair comparisons in multi-concept synthesis, we apply bounded attention [ 8 ] to CIDM [ 10 ] (denoted as BoundAtt) and incorporate regionally controllable sampling [ 17 ] into the other baselines. Since bounded attention is specifically designed for SDXL-based image generation, we only compare BoundAtt with our CCDM on SDXL-based text-to-image customization tasks under the CIVC setting. Evaluation Metrics: In this paper, we perform both qualitative and quantitative assessments on a variety of concept customization tasks, including single/multi-concept synthesis, editing, and style transfer across text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D domains [ 53 ] . 1) Single-Concept Quantitative Evaluation: We adopt image alignment (IA), text alignment (TA), forgetting of IA (FIA), and forgetting of TA (FTA) as evaluation metrics for text-to-image generation. Here, FIA = 1 U − 1 ​ ∑ i = 1 U − 1 ( IA i , i − IA i , U ) \mathrm{FIA}=\frac{1}{U-1}\sum_{i=1}^{U-1}\left(\mathrm{IA}_{i,i}-\mathrm{IA}_{i,U}\right) , where IA i , i \mathrm{IA}_{i,i} and IA i , U \mathrm{IA}_{i,U} denote the IA of the i i -th task evaluated after completing the learning of the i i -th and U U -th tasks, respectively. FTA = 1 U − 1 ​ ∑ i = 1 U − 1 ( TA i , i − TA i , U ) \mathrm{FTA}=\frac{1}{U-1}\sum_{i=1}^{U-1}\left(\mathrm{TA}_{i,i}-\mathrm{TA}_{i,U}\right) , where TA i , i \mathrm{TA}_{i,i} and TA i , U \mathrm{TA}_{i,U} represent the TA of the i i -th task measured after learning the i i -th and U U -th tasks, respectively. Besides, each concept is tested using 20 diverse prompts, each accompanied by a consistent negative prompt, with 25 samples generated per prompt. This results in 500 images per concept for evaluating IA, TA, FIA, and FTA. For text-to-video customization, inspired by [ 71 ] , we introduce an additional metric, DINOI (DI), alongside IA, TA, FIA, and FTA. For evaluation, we construct 10 distinct prompts for each concept and produce 10 video samples per prompt, yielding an aggregate of 100 generated videos per concept. To assess the performance on text-to-3D concept customization, we employ 20 diverse prompts for each learned concept, generating 25 samples per prompt, resulting in a total of 500 synthesized 3D assets per concept. Following [ 53 , 51 ] , we calculate the scores of IA, TA, FIA, and FTA using 40 uniformly distributed azimuth renderings at a fixed elevation angle of 40 degrees. These diverse metrics enable rigorous evaluation across various customization tasks in CIVC. 2) Multi-Concept Quantitative Evaluation: To assess the generalization of multi-concept synthesis, we conduct quantitative evaluation on two- and three-concept generation. Specifically, we randomly sample 10 concept pairs and 10 concept triplets to generate 20 concept combinations. Each combination is associated with 10 different prompts and corresponding bounding boxes, resulting in 200 distinct settings. For each setting, we generate 25 samples, yielding a total of 5,000 samples. Then, we crop the generated multi-concept samples into single-concept samples based on their bounding boxes, and evaluate them using the single-concept quantitative evaluation protocol.

sections.text: This subsection analyzes the efficacy of our CCDM in handling inter-object physical interactions during multi-concept generation with overlapping bounding boxes. As presented in Fig. 19 , in contrast to existing competing baselines that struggle to jointly generate multiple personalized concepts in a coherent manner, the proposed model effectively addresses the issue of concept neglect in user-specified overlapping bounding boxes by leveraging our controllable regional context synthesis module. These comparative results verify the effectiveness and robustness of our model in addressing inter-object physical interactions ( i.e. , overlapping bounding boxes) by enforcing clear semantic separation between different bounding boxes while ensuring seamless blending along their borders. They also demonstrate that the proposed controllable regional context synthesis module can effectively improve the overall coherence and harmony of multi-concept text-to-image compositions, even when the bounding boxes of different personalized concepts overlap.

sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: This paper presents a novel Continually Customizable Diffusion Model (CCDM) that effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect in Concept-Incremental Versatile Customization (CIVC). On one hand, to address the catastrophic forgetting of previously learned concepts, we devise an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module and a relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy. These two components preserve distinctive concept attributes while leveraging inter-task correlations to incrementally learn new customization tasks. On the other hand, to mitigate concept neglect, we introduce a controllable regional context synthesis module that composes multiple personalized concepts in accordance with user-specified requirements. This strategy enhances the overall quality of multi-concept synthesis by maintaining semantic independence across different regions and ensuring their smooth boundary blending. Through comprehensive evaluations, we validate our CCDM’s superiority over existing baselines in diverse CIVC scenarios spanning text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D domains. In future work, we will explore more robust memory mechanisms to retain long-term personalized knowledge and incorporate real-time user feedback to guide concept customization.

Jiahua Dong Wenqi Liang Hongliu Li Yang Cong Duzhen Zhang Hanbin Zhao Affiliation: Henghui Ding, Yulun Zhang, Salman Khan, Fahad Shahbaz Khan Abstract Custom diffusion models (CDMs) have garnered significant interest owing to their remarkable capacity for generating personalized concepts. However, the majority of CDMs unrealistically presume that the user’s collection of personalized concepts is static and incapable of incremental growth over time. Furthermore, they exhibit significant catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect of previously learned concepts when incrementally learning a sequence of new ones. To resolve the above challenges, we develop a novel C ontinually C ustomizable D iffusion M odel (CCDM), enabling users to perform concept-incremental versatile customization. Specifically, we design an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module and a relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. They can preserve concept-specific attributes of each task and leverage beneficial inter-task correlations to enhance the continual learning of new customization tasks. Additionally, to address the challenge of concept neglect, we propose a controllable regional context synthesis strategy that performs multi-concept composition in alignment with user-provided conditions. This strategy enhances the overall consistency in multi-concept synthesis by guaranteeing semantic independence between user-defined regions and their smooth boundary transitions. Experiments show our CCDM exhibits significant improvements over baseline methods. Index Terms: Versatile Concept Customization, Continual Learning, Catastrophic Forgetting, Concept Neglect. I Introduction Latent diffusion models (LDMs) [ 50 , 79 , 24 ] have emerged as an effective approach for high-quality content generation across various domains, including text-to-image synthesis [ 88 ] , video generation [ 76 ] , and 3D object creation [ 83 ] . By encoding input data into a latent space using a pretrained autoencoder, LDMs perform the denoising-based diffusion process in a lower-dimensional domain [ 47 ] . This design significantly reduces computational and memory costs while preserving the semantic richness required for photorealistic generation [ 28 , 21 ] . Despite their impressive performance, standard LDMs are typically trained on large-scale, general-purpose datasets [ 46 , 68 ] and struggle to synthesize user-specific concepts without extensive retraining. To address this limitation, custom diffusion models (CDMs) [ 82 , 25 , 44 , 20 ] have become a promising paradigm by using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 23 ] to finetune LDMs [ 46 , 3 ] on users’ personalized concepts. They expand the visual-language vocabulary of pretrained LDMs [ 88 ] by associating user-defined concepts with desired subjects [ 52 , 34 ] . Fig. 1: Illustration of the proposed CIVC problem. Fig. 2: Demonstration of our model’s scalability in supporting versatile concept customization tasks, including single/multi-concept synthesis, editing, and style transfer across text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D domains under the CIVC problem. Typically, the majority of CDMs [ 56 , 77 , 49 ] are built on the assumption that the set of each user’s personalized concepts remains constant and cannot continuously expand over time. However, this assumption contradicts practical scenarios, where users require a growing collection of new personalized concepts and wish to continually generate new concepts to reflect their evolving life experiences. To address such scenarios, existing CDMs [ 5 , 39 , 43 , 26 ] often rely on retaining all training data of previously learned concepts and leverage LoRA [ 23 ] to finetune pretrained LDMs [ 37 , 24 , 76 ] . Yet, as the volume of learned concepts accumulates, this strategy renders CDMs increasingly computationally intensive and more vulnerable to serious privacy issues [ 65 ] . If existing CDMs store all previously acquired low-rank parameters associated with old concepts and linearly fuse them for the continual learning of new concepts [ 78 , 90 ] , they may suffer from substantial degradation in their ability to preserve the distinctive characteristics of old personalized concepts, thereby hindering versatile concept customization [ 60 ] . This phenomenon is widely known as catastrophic forgetting of previously learned concepts [ 18 ] . Furthermore, in practical applications, users often seek precise control over the subjects and contexts linked to multiple previously learned concepts within generated images, videos, or 3D scenes for multi-concept composition, using conditions they provide (such as bounding boxes and scribbles [ 17 ] ). This requirement poses a significant challenge to CDMs [ 82 ] , which frequently face the issue of concept neglect [ 4 ] , whereby certain old concepts fail to appear during the synthesis of multiple concepts. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , CIVC enables CDMs [ 52 ] to continually learn and generate a series of new personalized concepts in a concept-incremental manner, while also supporting versatile concept customization tasks, including single/multi-concept synthesis, editing and style transfer across text-to-image [ 92 ] , text-to-video [ 26 ] and text-to-3D [ 44 ] domains. Our work significantly differs from existing baselines and offers strong scalability to perform a variety of different concept customization tasks (see Tab. I ). Additionally, during multi-concept composition, it allows users to guide the generation process by specifying the desired contexts, objects, and their intended spatial locations. Overall, the CIVC problem proposed in this paper faces the following two challenges: • Catastrophic Forgetting refers to the substantial loss of unique attributes of old concepts when existing CDMs [ 56 , 49 , 78 ] linearly merge their low-rank weights to incrementally learn new concepts. If new concepts ( e.g. , golden retriever) are semantically similar to previously learned ones ( e.g. , labrador retriever), CDMs tend to exhibit more severe forgetting of those old concepts. • Concept Neglect indicates the failure of some intended concepts to be properly synthesized at user-specified spatial locations during multi-concept composition. As multiple personalized concepts are composed together within generated images, videos, or 3D scenes, the risk increases that certain concepts may be overlooked, incorrectly blended, or visually overshadowed by others. To address the challenges of catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect in CIVC, we propose a novel C ontinually C ustomizable D iffusion M odel (CCDM) in this work. Firstly , we develop an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module and a relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy to alleviate catastrophic forgetting of previous concepts. The AD-LoRA module is designed to automatically retain concept-specific attributes while filtering out redundant characteristics. This is achieved by masking the LoRA parameters corresponding to irrelevant properties. By assessing semantic relevance, the relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy dynamically fuses low-rank updates from both current and previous tasks, exploiting beneficial inter-task correlations to facilitate the continual learning of new customization tasks. Secondly , to address concept neglect during multi-concept composition, we design a controllable regional context synthesis strategy that controls generated contexts to meet user-specified conditions. This module leverages a unified attention mask to restrict self-attention among image features exclusively to user-specified concept regions, while allowing cross-attention from image features to the textual embeddings of those regions. It promotes semantic independence across regions and seamless transitions at their boundaries, enhancing the holistic consistency of multi-concept synthesis. Comprehensive evaluations verify the efficacy of our CCDM in addressing diverse CIVC tasks across text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D domains (see Fig. 2 ). Our core contributions are listed as follows: • We formulate a practical Concept-Incremental Versatile Customization (CIVC) problem, characterized by challenges like catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect. • We design a novel Continually Customizable Diffusion Model (CCDM) to tackle the challenges of CIVC, enabling the continual customization of new concepts. • We propose attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) and relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation to alleviate catastrophic forgetting by retaining concept-specific attributes and exploiting positive inter-task correlations. • We develop a controllable regional context synthesis strategy to mitigate concept neglect in multi-concept generation by enabling semantic independence across regions and smooth transitions at their boundaries. Building upon our prior research [ 10 ] , this paper presents substantial improvements in both methodology and experiments: 1) Compared with [ 10 ] , we propose a novel attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module to identify which attributes of personalized concepts are distinctive. This AD-LoRA module preserves only the unique concept attributes to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. 2) The relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation merges the low-rank updates from current and previous tasks based on their semantic relevance. It explores positive inter-task relations to facilitate continual learning of new tasks. 3) We devise a controllable regional context synthesis strategy that uses a unified attention mask to limit self-attention to user-defined regions while enabling cross-attention to their textual embeddings for multi-concept synthesis. In contrast to [ 10 ] , it promotes greater semantic independence across regions and smoother transitions at their boundaries to tackle concept neglect. 4) We extend [ 10 ] to diverse CIVC tasks spanning text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D domains. 5) Our CCDM reduces the trainable parameters of [ 10 ] by 35% but achieves better customization performance than [ 10 ] . 6) More comparative evaluations, ablation results, and in-depth analyses are presented to prove the efficacy of our CCDM in handling the CIVC problem. II Related Work Continual Learning (CL) [ 73 , 12 , 70 ] allows AI systems to continuously accumulate new knowledge from a stream of tasks while preserving previously learned information [ 1 ] . Modern regularization approaches impose optimization constraints on the weight updates of previous tasks to maintain previously learned knowledge [ 29 , 36 ] or apply knowledge distillation to facilitate knowledge propagation between new and old models [ 11 ] . Additionally, data replay methods maintain exemplars from previous categories [ 1 , 9 ] , or leverage generative architectures to synthesize data representing old classes [ 73 ] . These methods retrain AI systems from scratch using a combination of new-class data and synthesized data from old classes. Dynamic architectural approaches progressively adapt their structures to continually assimilate new classes [ 86 , 12 ] , while representation-based methods utilize prompt learning [ 70 ] or contrastive learning [ 45 ] to alleviate forgetting. Moreover, CL has been applied to a variety of vision tasks, including object recognition [ 86 ] , scene understanding [ 64 ] , and multi-modal reasoning [ 41 ] . Despite their effectiveness in visual domains, most CL methods [ 64 , 12 , 9 ] cannot be directly applied to solve the continual concept customization task ( e.g. , the CIVC problem). Concept Customization [ 91 , 5 , 3 , 43 , 71 ] refers to the process of extending pretrained LDMs [ 55 , 24 ] to generate user-defined personalized concepts. Following [ 56 ] , which addresses subject-driven synthesis by finetuning the full set of parameters in LDMs [ 3 ] , Gal et al. leverage textual inversion [ 14 ] to encode personalized concepts into learnable word embeddings for text-to-image concept customization. [ 30 ] enables the simultaneous training of multiple concepts or the merging of distinct diffusion models through the optimization of cross-attention parameters for multi-concept composition. Inspired by [ 30 ] , [ 19 ] optimizes only the singular value decomposition of latent encoding parameters to enhance customization efficiency. Building upon prior works [ 42 , 14 ] , some researchers [ 71 , 77 , 85 , 34 , 66 ] have extended these methodologies to temporal domains for personalized text-to-video synthesis. DreamVideo [ 71 ] proposes a dual-phase training strategy that separates concept acquisition from motion modeling, and [ 5 ] is designed for multi-concept video customization. For text-to-3D generation [ 80 , 39 ] , several works [ 53 , 51 , 52 , 83 ] use 2D LDMs [ 58 , 16 ] as the backbone and apply pose control to 3D objects, while others [ 49 , 44 , 81 ] aim to incorporate implicit 3D priors to facilitate the generation process. Besides, [ 60 , 62 , 18 ] focus on continual customization tasks that continuously synthesize new concepts, yet they lack the ability to control generated contexts and are prone to concept neglect during multi-concept synthesis. To tackle this issue, [ 88 , 47 ] use regional conditions, such as bounding boxes, to guide composition. However, the above CDMs [ 20 , 30 , 80 ] fail to incrementally synthesize new concepts in CIVC scenarios, suffering from catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect. III Preliminary and Problem Definition Preliminary: To steer the generation of images, latent diffusion models (LDMs) [ 58 , 79 , 16 , 55 ] utilize conditional cues such as textual descriptions or images. The diffusion process takes places in a latent space, where an encoder ℰ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{E}(\cdot) transforms inputs into latent representations, and a decoder 𝒟 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{D}(\cdot) reconstructs them into images. By finetuning pretrained LDMs [ 59 , 50 ] with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 23 , 40 ] , custom diffusion models (CDMs) [ 42 , 43 , 91 ] can learn user-specific concepts. Nevertheless, existing CDMs [ 81 , 14 ] typically presume a fixed set of user-specific concepts, which does not align with practical scenarios where users often desire to consecutively incorporate new personalized concepts reflecting their evolving preferences [ 60 ] . Additionally, these models are notably vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting of previously learned concepts and the neglect of certain concepts [ 62 , 42 ] when adapting to an incrementally expanding set of personalized concepts for versatile customization [ 10 ] . Problem Definition: To tackle the aforementioned issues, this paper introduces an innovative problem termed Concept-Incremental Versatile Customization (CIVC). This problem involves a sequence of successive concept customization tasks, denoted as 𝒯 = { 𝒯 u } u = 1 U \mathcal{T}=\{\mathcal{T}_{u}\}_{u=1}^{U} , with U U indicating the total number of tasks. The u u -th task 𝒯 u = { 𝐱 u s , 𝐩 u s , 𝐲 u s } s = 1 N u \mathcal{T}_{u}=\{\mathbf{x}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{p}_{u}^{s},\mathbf{y}_{u}^{s}\}_{s=1}^{N_{u}} comprises N u N_{u} triplet samples, each containing an image 𝐱 u s \mathbf{x}_{u}^{s} , a corresponding text prompt 𝐩 u s \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s} , and a concept token 𝐲 u s ∈ 𝒴 u \mathbf{y}_{u}^{s}\in\mathcal{Y}_{u} . Specifically, the text prompt 𝐩 u s \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s} describes the visual content of 𝐱 u s \mathbf{x}_{u}^{s} ( e.g. , “photo of a [ V ∗ V_{*} ] [ V cat V_{\mathrm{cat}} ] drinking a cup of beer”), while 𝐲 u s \mathbf{y}_{u}^{s} is the conceptual element (such as [ V ∗ V_{*} ] [ V cat V_{\mathrm{cat}} ]) extracted from 𝐩 u s \mathbf{p}_{u}^{s} . The concept space 𝒴 u \mathcal{Y}_{u} for the u u -th learning task contains C u C_{u} new concepts, defined as 𝐲 u = ∪ s = 1 N u 𝐲 u s \mathbf{y}_{u}=\cup_{s=1}^{N_{u}}\mathbf{y}_{u}^{s} . In the CIVC setting, the concept spaces of distinct tasks are completely disjoint: 𝒴 u ∩ ( ∪ i = 1 u − 1 𝒴 i ) = ∅ \mathcal{Y}_{u}\cap(\cup_{i=1}^{u{-}1}\mathcal{Y}_{i})=\emptyset . This indicates that the C u C_{u} new personalized concepts introduced in the u u -th task are entirely distinct from the K u − 1 = ∑ i = 1 u − 1 C i K_{u{-}1}=\sum_{i=1}^{u{-}1}C_{i} previous concepts accumulated from the preceding u − 1 u{-}1 tasks. As shown in Tab. 1 , based on individual user preferences, each task 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} belongs to one of the diverse customization tasks: single/multi-concept synthesis, editing and style transfer across text-to-image [ 19 ] , text-to-video [ 75 ] and text-to-3D [ 61 ] domains. This is also referred to as versatile customization, which is the main focus of this paper. To satisfy the practical requirements of CIVC, no memory is reserved for archiving or reconstructing the training sets { 𝒯 u } u = 1 U \{\mathcal{T}_{u}\}_{u=1}^{U} across all tasks. This design ensures that all customization tasks adhere strictly to the concept-incremental learning paradigm. The CIVC setting aims to facilitate continual learning of new personalized concepts to meet diverse customization needs, while effectively tackling catastrophic forgetting of previous concepts and the challenge of concept neglect. IV The Proposed Model In this section, as shown in Figs. 3 - 4 , we first use text-to-image customization as a representative example to illustrate the pipeline of our CCDM, which resolves the challenges of catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect in the CIVC problem. Specifically, we propose an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module (Sec. IV-A ) and a relevance-guided AD-LoRA aggregation strategy (Sec. IV-B ) to overcome catastrophic forgetting, while also designing a controllable regional context synthesis strategy (Sec. IV-C ) to alleviate concept neglect during multi-concept generation. Then, we discuss how to extend our CCDM to text-to-video (Sec. IV-D ) and text-to-3D (Sec. IV-E ) customization under the CIVC setting. Here, θ u ′ = θ 0 + Δ ​ θ u \theta^{\prime}_{u}=\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{u} , Δ ​ θ u = { Δ ​ 𝐖 u l } l = 1 L \Delta\theta_{u}=\{\Delta\mathbf{W}_{u}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L} , and Δ ​ 𝐖 u l = 𝐀 u l ​ 𝐁 u l ∈ ℝ a × b \Delta\mathbf{W}_{u}^{l}=\mathbf{A}_{u}^{l}\mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times b} represents the low-rank updates in the l l -th layer, with 𝐀 u l ∈ ℝ a × r \mathbf{A}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times r} and 𝐁 u l ∈ ℝ r × b \mathbf{B}_{u}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times b} being the corresponding low-rank decomposition matrices. Previous studies [ 55 , 82 ] have demonstrated that Δ ​ θ u \Delta\theta_{u} effectively captures the majority of the personalized concept characteristics in 𝒯 u \mathcal{T}_{u} . To continually learn new customization tasks under the CIVC setting, existing CDMs [ 27 , 69 , 53 ] require retaining the low-rank weights { Δ ​ θ i } i = 1 u − 1 \{\Delta\theta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{u-1} from all preceding tasks and linearly combining them during training by assessing their respective contributions to the current task. Unfortunately, this linear combination of low-rank weights causes a significant degradation in their ability to capture the distinctive attributes of previous concepts, a phenomenon also known as catastrophic forgetting of old concepts [ 18 ] . In light of this, Dong et al. [ 10 ] aim to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during model training by simultaneously preserving task-specific and shared knowledge through a concept consolidation loss. However, this method fails to identify which attributes of personalized concepts are distinctive and which are irrelevant in each incremental task. Moreover, the orthogonal constraint in [ 10 ] is highly dependent on hyperparameter selection, which cannot guarantee the absence of negative interference from irrelevant attributes across different tasks. Under these circumstances, mistakenly extracting irrelevant attributes of personalized concepts from previous tasks can severely interfere with the discovery of inherent attributes in the current customization task, thereby exacerbating forgetting under the CIVC setting. To address the above issues, as shown in Fig. 3 , we propose layer-wise concept tokens to explore a wide range of diverse attributes for personalized concepts. Additionally, we develop an attribute-decoupled LoRA (AD-LoRA) module that selectively preserves task-specific distinctive attributes while discarding irrelevant properties by zeroing out their encoding parameters in the low-rank weights.
